name: Murata-grm_GRM31C5C1H224JE02
title: GRM31C5C1H224JE02: 0.22 µF, 50 V DC, C0G multilayer ceramic chip capacitor, 3216M (1206)
summary: A 0.22 µF ±5% chip multilayer ceramic capacitor of the GRM series, built on the C0G (5C) dielectric and rated 50 V DC. The body measures 3.2 × 1.6 × 1.6 mm (3216M, EIA 1206) and carries a termination at each end; it takes either reflow or flow soldering. It runs from -55 to 125 ℃ and is intended for consumer, industrial, non-implant medical and automotive infotainment equipment.

operation.text: Four classes of equipment are inside the specification. Consumer: household appliances, audio and video gear, communication, information and office machines, and robots for the home. Industrial: base stations, production machinery, industrial robots, measuring instruments. Medical: GHTF class A and class B devices, and class C devices other than implants. Automotive: infotainment and comfort gear, car navigation and car audio among them, for which no law sets a technical standard of safety or environmental protection. In all four the part's function does not bear directly on protecting life or property.

Eleven classes of equipment fall outside the specific application: aircraft, aerospace, undersea, power-plant control, medical, transportation, traffic-control, disaster-prevention and security, industrial data-processing, and combustion and explosion control equipment, together with anything of like complexity or demanded reliability. Murata disclaims loss and damage arising from use in any of them unless such use is named as a specific application.

Temperature characteristic 5C is the EIA class C0G: between 25 and 125 ℃, referred to 25 ℃, the capacitance moves by 0 ±30 ppm/℃. Below the reference temperature the allowed change is set out in Table A. Across the temperature steps the drift stays within ±0.2% or ±0.05 pF, whichever is the larger.

50 V DC is the most that may sit across the part continuously. Where an AC component rides on DC the zero-to-peak value must stay at or below 50 V; with AC or pulse voltage the peak-to-peak value must. Surge, static-electricity and pulse voltages are held to the same limit. Overvoltage breaks down the internal dielectric layers and shorts the part, after a time that depends on the voltage and on the ambient temperature.

Measure at the frequency and voltage the specification gives: 1.0 ±0.1 kHz at 1.0 ±0.2 Vrms. On high-capacitance parts the meter's output voltage can sag, so check that the prescribed voltage actually reaches the part. High dielectric constant types read differently with the AC level applied, which matters when the part goes into an AC circuit.

AC or pulse current through the part heats it through dielectric loss, so the surface temperature including that rise must stay inside the operating range. For parts rated under 100 V DC the load is held so that self-heating of the body stays below 20 °C measured at a 25 °C ambient.

High dielectric constant types (X7R, X5R and the like) lose capacitance under DC bias, shift with the AC level and with temperature, and age downward with time; a tight-tolerance circuit such as a time constant has to allow for all of it, checked in the real system.

Keep reels at +5 to +40 ℃ and 20 to 70 %RH, preferably under 30 ℃, out of direct sunlight and away from condensation and from corrosive gases such as hydrogen sulfide, sulfur dioxide, chlorine and ammonia, which attack the terminations and spoil solderability. Long or hot, damp storage degrades the packaging and oxidises the electrodes: after six months check the packaging and mounting, after a year the solderability as well.

Mount the part where it will not sit at a resonance and where nothing strikes its terminals. A drop can crack the dielectric, and a dropped part is not used again. Boards stacked or carried loose can let one board's corner strike a capacitor on another.

Place the chip so that board flexing stresses it as little as possible: lay it across the direction in which the stress acts, keep it away from board separation lines and from screw holes, and where it has to sit near a separation line, add slits there. Parts taken off equipment are not reused, and Sn-Zn solder lowers MLCC reliability. A part held in long storage takes a heat treatment before its capacitance is measured.

Set the lowest point of the pickup nozzle so that it does not bend the board, and keep the nozzle, its suction path and the locating claws clean and replaced on schedule; dirt in the suction path or a worn claw presses unevenly and cracks chips.

Preheat both the board and the parts so that the step from the component surface to the solder, ΔT, stays within 190 ℃ for the 31 size, and keep the same ΔT between a hot assembly and any solvent it is dipped in afterwards. Peak 240 to 260 ℃ in air or nitrogen with Sn-3.0Ag-0.5Cu. Soldering below the peak the solder maker specifies risks poor wetting, voids, whiskering, weak bonds, poor self-alignment and tombstoning or shifting on the lands. Too much paste raises the fillet and passes board stress into the chip; too little leaves the termination weakly held.

Flow soldering is allowed only for the 155, 18, 21 and 31 sizes, with ΔT up to 150 ℃, a preheat peak of 100 to 120 ℃ and a solder peak of 250 to 260 ℃. Too long or too hot a dwell leaches the terminations, which weakens adhesion and can lower capacitance as the inner electrodes lose contact. The top of the fillet should stay below the chip's thickness.

Preheat the board to at least 150 ℃, keep the iron at 350 ℃ max. for the 31 size, work quickly and let the board cool slowly. Use an iron tip of ø3 mm or smaller that never touches the chip, and solder wire of ø0.5 mm or smaller. A spot heater heats part and board together and is gentler: nozzle 5 mm or more away, hot air at 45°, 400 °C max. at the outlet, under 10 s on chips up to 3.2 × 1.6 mm.

Too much ultrasonic power sets the board resonating, which cracks chips and breaks solder joints; qualify the cleaning equipment and process on real parts first. A test probe pushing on a loaded board flexes it and cracks chips or opens joints, so put support pins behind the board as near the probe as they will go, and keep the probe from striking the board hard enough to shake it.

Once the part is on the board, bending or twisting the board cracks it, and a cracked part loses insulation resistance and may short. Separate with a jig or a machine rather than by hand or nippers. The router type stresses the board least, the board staying flat under the spinning cutter. With a jig, hold the board near the jig and bend it toward the face the parts are on. A disc separator needs its top and bottom blades aligned in all three directions and its V groove cut to the right angle and depth, neither so shallow that the board resists nor so deep that it breaks in handling. On a double-sided board, prefer a router; failing that, lay the parts parallel to the separation surface, add slits near any part close to it, and keep parts away from the separation point.

Held in one hand a loaded board bends, so take it by both edges with both hands, and do not use a board that has been dropped. Mounting parts on the far side afterwards, set the nozzle's bottom dead point on the surface of a straightened board and check it from time to time, or the board deflects and cracks the parts underneath. Before pressing in a transformer, an IC or another leaded part, enlarge the lead holes and hold the board on support pins or in a dedicated jig, the pins all at one height. Fitting or pulling sockets and connectors warps the board as well. Plan screw tightening so the board does not bend, and use a torque screwdriver; a board left bowed by reflow passes that stress to the chips if screws flatten it.

Where the chip is glued down before flow soldering, the adhesive, the amount, the contact area, the land size and the curing schedule all bear on the result. Too little adhesive or a short or cool cure leaves the part loose; too much runs onto the land and spoils the joint; too hot or too long a cure weakens the bond and oxidises the terminations and the land. Epoxy is the usual choice, and it should hold through the process and through soldering moisture, coat and keep its shape, have a long pot life and a short cure, not corrode chip or board, insulate well, give off nothing harmful and carry no halogenated compounds.

Apply flux thinly and evenly: too much gives off a lot of flux gas and spoils solderability, and flux with more than 0.1% halide corrodes the terminations unless cleaning is thorough. Strongly acidic flux corrodes the part. Set the soldering temperature and time so that leaching of a termination stays within 25% of the chip end area and 25% of the mounted edge length.

A chip sits straight on the board, so it feels flexing and thermal stress more than a leaded part, and an over-tall solder fillet multiplies it: size the lands to keep the fillet low, and divide the land from a chassis, a neighbouring leaded part or wide copper with solder resist. A board whose thermal expansion is far from the chip's, such as fluorine resin or single-layer glass epoxy, can crack it. Moving to a smaller chip means revisiting the wiring width, the wiring direction and the copper thickness, not just the land.

Resin shrinking as it cures can crack the chip, so choose a low-shrinkage resin whose thermal expansion is close to the chip's; a silicone undercoat buffers the stress. Choose a resin that takes up little moisture, such as epoxy, since a hygroscopic one in humid air lowers insulation resistance. Coatings carrying halogen compounds or organic acids corrode the chip, so no strongly acidic type. Qualify the cleaning equipment and solvent on real parts; poor cleaning leaves flux residue that degrades the electrical characteristics and the reliability.
In an AC or pulse circuit a high dielectric constant type vibrates at certain frequencies and can make audible noise, and mechanical vibration or shock applied to it can do the same.

Do not touch a capacitor in a running circuit, let its terminals meet a conductor or a conductive liquid, or run it splashed with water or oil, in direct sunlight, in ozone, ultraviolet or radiation, in toxic gas, in condensation or beyond the vibration limits. Water or brine shorts the part, and moisture or corrosive gas on the terminals shortens its life. A cracked part may short, so a circuit where that could give a shock, smoke or fire needs a fail-safe such as a fuse. The series carries no safety-standard certification, and waste parts go to a licensed industrial waste contractor.

Carry the parts so that the outer boxes are not deformed and no force reaches the inner packaging, and keep them from excessive temperature, humidity, vibration, shock and pressure. A sharp edge, tweezers, an iron, an air driver or a chassis striking the body can chip or crack it and short it. Evaluate the part in the finished system, including leakage current and noise absorption, and check its surge withstand against the surges the system's inductance can produce.
